title: AI-Powered SDLC with Claude Code
bodyHtml:
Welcome to the AI-Powered SDLC workshop. This is a hands-on curriculum that maps Claude Code to every phase of the software development lifecycle — from understanding the tool's foundations through autonomous coding pipelines.

You will work with TaskFlow, a lightweight task management application, and progressively build real artifacts: requirements documents, architecture plans, tested implementations, and an autonomous coding pipeline — all powered by Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock.

Target Audience

This workshop is designed for software developers, tech leads, and architects who want to integrate AI-assisted development into their workflow. It is hands-on and code-focused — you will be writing prompts, creating configuration files, and building real features throughout.

Background Knowledge

Participants should be comfortable with:

  • Command-line basics — navigating directories, running commands in a terminal
  • JavaScript/Node.js fundamentals — the sample project uses Express.js, though deep JS expertise is not required
  • Git basics — clone, commit, branch (used for version control during exercises)
  • REST API concepts — HTTP methods, status codes, JSON request/response (the sample project is a REST API)

No prior experience with Claude Code or AI-assisted development is needed — the workshop teaches everything from the ground up.

Prerequisites

You need access to the workshop Code Editor environment — your facilitator will provide the URL. Everything else is pre-installed and ready.

This workshop uses Claude models hosted on Amazon Bedrock. Claude Code works seamlessly with Bedrock, so you get AI-assisted development within your existing AWS infrastructure, VPCs, and security boundaries.

Cost

When running this workshop at an AWS-hosted event, the environment is provided at no cost to participants. If you deploy the workshop infrastructure in your own AWS account, you will incur costs for the EC2 instance, CloudFront distribution, and Amazon Bedrock model usage. See Amazon Bedrock pricing  and Amazon EC2 pricing  for details. Remember to delete the CloudFormation stack when you are done to stop incurring charges.

Click Introduction to learn what this workshop covers, or jump straight to Getting Started if you are ready to begin.

title: Introduction
bodyHtml:
The "L" in SDLC stands for lifecycle — each phase's output is the next phase's input. This workshop takes that literally. Requirements become stories. Stories become a backlog. The backlog becomes a spec. The spec drives tests. Tests drive implementation. Implementation gets automated by a pipeline.

The Artifact Chain

Every phase produces a durable file that feeds the next:

Raw sources → Structured notes → Requirements → User stories → Backlog → Spec → Architecture → Tests → Implementation → Autonomous pipeline

Nothing lives only in chat. Everything is committed to files. When a session ends, the work survives — and when the workshop ends, your taskflow/ repo contains every artifact above, plus a reusable Ralph pipeline that can build the next feature from your backlog on its own.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this workshop, you will be able to:

  • Understand how Claude Code works — the agentic loop, context window, tools, sub-agents, and Plan Mode
  • Configure Claude Code for your team — CLAUDE.md, settings, path-scoped rules, and auto memory
  • Extend Claude Code — build custom agents, skills, hooks, and MCP integrations
  • Apply Claude Code across the full SDLC — requirements engineering, system design, TDD implementation, and self-review
  • Build an autonomous coding pipeline — the Ralph Loop, a bash-driven pipeline that builds features from your backlog without interactive prompting

Workshop Structure

SectionWhat You Will Do
Getting StartedConnect to your Code Editor, clone TaskFlow, start Claude Code
Claude Code FoundationThe agentic loop, context, tools, sub-agents, Plan Mode, golden rules
Claude Code ConfigurationCLAUDE.md, settings, rules, auto memory
Claude Code ExtensionsSkills, agents, hooks, MCP, agent teams, recap
SDLC 1-4Requirements, Design, Implementation, Ralph Loop
ConclusionReview artifacts, next steps, cleanup

title: Claude Code Foundation
bodyHtml: How Claude Code actually works — the engine room every participant must understand. This section covers the mental model, the agentic loop, tools, sub-agents, Plan Mode, and the principles that keep you productive.

images.alt: The agentic loop: Gather context, Take action, Verify results — with the human in the loop to interrupt, steer, or add context

title: The Mindset Shift
bodyHtml:
Here is the mental model that will serve you for the rest of this workshop: Claude Code is a terminal-native agentic assistant. You are the architect. Claude is your execution engine. Think of yourself as a tech lead who just hired an extremely fast, extremely knowledgeable engineer — you describe the task, point them at the codebase, and review their work.

You do not write the code. You do not tell Claude which files to open or which commands to run. Instead, you describe what you want at the level of intent — "add authentication to this API," "refactor this module to use dependency injection," "find and fix the race condition in the checkout flow" — and Claude figures out how to make it happen. Your job is to set direction, review results, and make decisions. Claude's job is to read, understand, plan, execute, and verify.

The Agentic Loop

Every AI agent needs a control loop — the mechanism that decides what to do next. Most agent frameworks build elaborate orchestration: decision trees, routing classifiers, retrieval pipelines, state machines. Claude Code does none of that. Its architecture is radically simple: one loop, three phases, driven entirely by the model's own reasoning.

This simplicity is not a limitation. It is a deliberate design choice by Anthropic, and understanding it will change how you think about what Claude Code can and cannot do.

The three phases

Source: How Claude Code works  — Anthropic

Every task Claude Code performs follows this same cycle. When you give it an instruction, it first gathers context — reading files, searching your codebase with grep and glob, checking documentation. It builds a mental model of what exists before touching anything. Then it takes action — editing files, writing new code, running shell commands. Finally, it verifies its own work — running tests, checking for errors, validating that the output matches your intent.

This cycle repeats. If verification reveals a problem, Claude gathers more context about the failure, takes corrective action, and verifies again. The loop continues until the task is complete or Claude needs your input to proceed.

The loop in pseudocode

while (task_not_complete) {
  context = gather(read, glob, grep, webfetch)
  result  = act(edit, write, bash)
  status  = verify(run_tests, check_output)
  if (status === 'needs_human') break
}

TRY IT: Feel the difference — intent vs. instructions

Try two different prompting styles for the same goal and compare how Claude responds.

Before you start

Make sure you have completed Getting Started > TaskFlow Setup and Meet Claude Code. You should have TaskFlow running in one terminal tab and Claude Code running in a second terminal tab. If not, go back and complete those steps first.

Open src/server.js in your editor. Notice how the code has almost no comments — about 25 lines of raw Express wiring with zero documentation. Keep that in mind for what follows.

Step 1 — Micro-managed prompt (anti-pattern): Micromanage Claude — tell it exactly what to do:

Open src/server.js. Find the line with app.listen. Add a comment above it
that says "// Start the server".

Observe: Claude does exactly what you asked — nothing more. It acts as a typist, not a thinker.

Step 2 — Intent-driven prompt: Now describe intent instead — tell Claude what you want, not how:

This codebase has almost no code comments. Add useful documentation comments
to the most important files — focus on anything a new developer would need
to understand.

Observe: Claude explores the codebase on its own, decides which files matter, and adds meaningful comments. The intent-driven prompt produced better results because Claude used its own judgment about what mattered. You described the outcome; Claude figured out the path. This is the paradigm shift — from "writing code with AI help" to "orchestrating an AI that writes code." The instinct to micromanage is strong. Resist it.

title: Context and Tools
bodyHtml:
The context window determines what Claude can see — your conversation history, files it has read, tool outputs, and system instructions. Understanding it helps you work effectively in longer sessions.

What fills the context window

The latest Claude models support up to 1 million tokens of context. That is enormous — enough to hold large codebases, lengthy conversations, and extensive tool output simultaneously. The context is filled by:

  • System prompt and tool definitions — fixed overhead from Claude Code's built-in instructions and configured MCP servers
  • CLAUDE.md files and rules — your project instructions, loaded at session start
  • Conversation history — everything you and Claude have said this session
  • File contents — files Claude has read into context
  • Command outputs — terminal output from bash, test runs, builds

TRY IT: Check your context

Run /context to see how your context window is being used:

/context

Observe: You see a breakdown of what is consuming your context window. Here is what each category means:

CategoryWhat it is
System promptClaude Code's built-in instructions — always present, you cannot change this
System toolsDefinitions for the 8 built-in tools (Read, Edit, Bash, etc.) so Claude knows how to use them
SkillsReusable workflow templates — you will create these later in the Extensions section
MessagesYour conversation so far — every prompt you typed and every response Claude gave
Free spaceAvailable room for more conversation, file reads, and tool output
Autocompact bufferReserved space — when context fills up, Claude automatically compresses older messages to make room

Right now, most of your context is free space. As you work — reading files, getting responses, running commands — the Messages category will grow. The key number to watch is the total percentage at the top.

Managing context in long sessions

Even with 1M tokens, very long sessions eventually accumulate enough history that older context gets compressed. Claude Code handles this automatically through auto-compaction — summarizing older conversation turns to make room for new ones. You can also compact manually:

  • /compact — summarize and compress the conversation so far (use between tasks, not mid-task)
  • /clear — reset the conversation completely
  • /context — check current usage

For most workshop exercises, context management is not a concern — sessions are short and focused. It becomes important in real-world use when you have long, multi-hour development sessions. The key habit: compact at logical breakpoints between tasks, not in the middle of one.

The Eight Built-in Tools

Claude Code has exactly eight built-in tools. No plugin marketplace, no extension ecosystem at the base layer. Just eight carefully chosen primitives that, in combination, can accomplish virtually any software engineering task.

IconNameDescription
📖ReadRead file contents
🔍GlobFind files by pattern
🔎GrepSearch file contents
🌐WebFetchFetch URLs
✍️WriteCreate new files
✏️EditEdit existing files
💻BashRun shell commands
🤖TaskSpawn sub-agents

TRY IT: Ask Claude which tools it just used

In the previous exercise (Mindset Shift), you asked Claude to add comments to the most important files — an open-ended, intent-driven task. Claude reached for several of these tools on its own. Ask it to walk you through that decision:

Which tools did you just use to complete the commenting task, and why in that order?

Observe: Claude will describe its own escalation — typically Glob or Read to orient in the project, then Grep to find undocumented code, then Read to dive into the files that matter, and finally Edit to add the comments. You never told Claude which tools to pick. It reasoned about what was efficient given the intent you described.

The search strategy: how Claude explores your code

When Claude needs to understand your codebase — whether to fix a bug, add a feature, or answer a question — it follows a natural escalation pattern. This is not hardcoded logic; it emerges from the model's own reasoning about efficiency. But it is remarkably consistent:

🔍 Glob (Find files by pattern) → 🔎 Grep (Search content across files) → 📖 Read (Read files deeply) → 🤖 Task (Delegate to sub-agent)

First, Glob to discover what files exist and where. Then Grep to search across those files for relevant content. Then Read to dive deep into the files that matter. And if the exploration is large or tangential, Task to delegate it to a sub-agent so the main context stays clean.

This "Search, Don't Index" approach trades a small amount of latency for significant advantages: no index to keep in sync as code changes, no embedding pipeline to maintain, no security concerns from sending code to external services, and the guarantee that Claude is always searching your actual current code — not a stale snapshot.

title: Sub-Agents
bodyHtml:
As you work with Claude Code on real projects, you will encounter a recurring tension: you need Claude to explore something large or tangential, but you do not want that exploration to consume your main context window. Sub-agents solve this problem.

The Task tool spawns an isolated sub-agent — a completely separate Claude instance with its own fresh context window. It receives only the task description you provide, does its work using the same tools available to the main session, and returns a summary of its findings. The critical insight is that only that summary enters your main context. All the intermediate work — the files read, the searches performed, the reasoning — stays in the sub-agent's context and is discarded when it finishes.

Three agents do 90k tokens of work in parallel. Your session receives ~600 tokens of summaries. The agent contexts are discarded.

How sub-agents work

When Claude (or you) decides to use a sub-agent, here is what happens:

  1. A new Claude instance is created with a fresh context window.
  2. It receives only the task description — no conversation history, no previously read files, no accumulated context from the parent session.
  3. It has access to the same tools as the main session (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebFetch) — except it cannot spawn its own sub-agents.
  4. It works through the task autonomously, using the same Gather-Act-Verify loop.
  5. When finished, it returns a text summary to the parent session.
  6. Only that summary text is added to the parent's context window.

This isolation is the key feature. A sub-agent might read 30 files and run 15 grep searches to answer a question — that could be 50,000+ tokens of work. But only a few hundred tokens of summary come back to your main session.

Specialized agent types

Claude Code ships with five built-in sub-agent types, each optimized for a particular kind of work. Run /agents to see them in your own session — the Library tab lists all of them.

TypeTools AvailableBest For
ExploreRead-only (Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch)Fast codebase exploration. Supports a thoroughness setting — quick, medium, or very thorough
PlanRead-onlyArchitecture and implementation planning — returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, weighs trade-offs
general-purposeAll toolsOpen-ended research and multi-step tasks when you are not sure where to look
claude-code-guideGlob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearchAnswers questions about Claude Code, the Agent SDK, and the Claude API
statusline-setupRead, EditConfigures your Claude Code status line

Explore and Plan are the workhorses for keeping your main context clean. When you need to understand a large directory structure, trace a complex call chain, or design an approach before writing code, delegating to one of these agents means the investigation does not consume any of your precious main-session tokens.

Why depth is limited to one level

Sub-agents cannot spawn their own sub-agents. This depth=1 limitation is intentional and important:

  • Recursive explosion — without a depth limit, a poorly-scoped task could spawn agents that spawn agents indefinitely, consuming unbounded resources.
  • Cost predictability — each sub-agent consumes tokens. Nested agents make costs unpredictable and potentially very large.
  • Debuggability — when something goes wrong in a single-level sub-agent, you can reason about what happened. Multi-level agent chains become opaque quickly.
  • Reliability — each level of nesting introduces another point of failure. Keeping it flat keeps it reliable.

Think of sub-agents as disposable researchers — you send them on a focused mission, they come back with a report, and your main workspace stays clean.

TRY IT: Parallel sub-agents — three analyses at once

Sub-agents are not just about context isolation — they also run in parallel. You will ask Claude to investigate three different aspects of the codebase simultaneously, then see how little context it cost.

Step 1 — Check baseline: Check your current context usage:

1
/context

Observe: Note the total context percentage. This is your starting point.

Step 2 — Parallel sub-agent analysis: Now ask Claude to run three analyses in parallel using sub-agents:

Use sub-agents to analyze these three things in parallel:
1. What security vulnerabilities exist in the API routes?
2. What happens if two users modify the same task at the same time?
3. What would need to change to make this project production-ready?

Observe: Watch the terminal — Claude spawns three Task agents simultaneously. You can see them working in parallel, each searching and reading files independently. They finish one by one, each returning a focused summary. Three analyses in the time it would take one to complete sequentially.

Step 3 — Check after sub-agents: Now check your context usage:

1
/context

Observe: Context barely moved. Three separate analyses — security, concurrency, production readiness — each reading multiple files and reasoning deeply, yet your main session only received the summaries. Sub-agents give you parallelism and context efficiency at once. This is the pattern for any exploratory work — delegate to sub-agents, keep your main session clean for decision-making.

title: Plan Mode and Power Features
bodyHtml:
One of the most common mistakes new Claude Code users make is jumping straight into execution. You describe a feature, Claude starts editing files, and ten minutes later you realize it went in a direction you did not want. Rolling back is possible but painful. The solution is Plan Mode — a simple but powerful mechanism that forces Claude to think before it acts.

Plan Mode: read-only exploration

Plan Mode is activated by pressing Shift+Tab until you see the Plan indicator. In this mode, Claude can do everything it normally does except modify your codebase. It can read files, search code, analyze architecture, and reason about approaches — but it cannot write, edit, or execute commands that change state.

What it produces instead is a plan: a numbered, structured checklist of exactly what it intends to do. You review this plan, refine it if needed ("skip step 3, and do step 5 before step 4"), and then switch back to normal mode where Claude executes the approved plan.

Boris Cherny, the engineering lead for Claude Code at Anthropic, has stated that he uses Plan Mode for approximately 80% of his tasks. Even the person who builds the tool prefers to have Claude think before it acts most of the time. Plan Mode is not just for complex tasks — even simple changes benefit from a quick plan.

TRY IT: Plan first, then execute

Use Plan Mode to explore and plan a feature, then switch to execution mode. You will see the difference between Claude thinking and Claude acting.

Step 1 — Fresh start: Start with a clean session — the previous exercises filled up context:

1
/clear

Observe: Context is reset. You have a full context budget for this exercise.

Step 2 — Switch to Plan Mode: IMPORTANT: Before typing anything, press Shift+Tab to cycle into Plan Mode. You should see a Plan indicator in the status bar. This switches Claude to read-only mode — it can explore and reason but cannot modify any files.

Run in terminal:

1
Shift+Tab

Observe: The status bar now shows Plan mode. Claude will not write, edit, or execute any commands that change your project.

Step 3 — Prompt to Claude (in Plan Mode): Now ask Claude to plan a feature that touches both the backend and the frontend:

The kanban board has no search. The API already supports ?search= on
GET /api/tasks, but there's no search bar in the UI. Add a search input
above the columns that filters tasks as you type. Plan the implementation.

Observe: Claude reads the route files and the frontend HTML but makes no edits. It produces a numbered plan — likely covering where to add the search input, how to wire it to the API or do client-side filtering, and how to update the board. Notice that Claude makes design decisions (client-side vs API filtering) without being told which to choose.

When Claude finishes the plan, you will see a prompt asking how to proceed:

You have three options:

  • Option 1 (Yes, auto-accept edits) — Claude implements the plan and auto-approves all file changes
  • Option 2 (Yes, manually approve edits) — Claude implements but asks your permission before each edit
  • Option 3 (Tell Claude what to change) — Refine the plan before executing

Step 4 — Refine the plan: Choose option 3 to give feedback before executing. Type your refinement:

Good plan. But do client-side filtering instead of calling the API
on every keystroke — we already have all tasks loaded. Also add a
clear button to reset the search.

Observe: Claude revises the plan to include your refinements without touching any files. You are having a design conversation, not a coding session. When it presents the updated plan, choose option 1 (auto-accept) to let Claude implement it.

If you prefer to skip the refinement, choose option 1 directly at the first prompt — Claude will implement the original plan as-is.

Observe: Claude follows its own plan step by step — adding the search input, wiring the filtering logic, styling it to match the existing board. Because the plan was solid, the implementation is structured and predictable.

Step 6 — Verify visually: If your TaskFlow server is still running in the other terminal tab, just refresh the browser window. If you stopped it earlier, switch to that terminal tab and run npm run dev again — it will reopen the app.

Observe: The Kanban board now has a search bar. Type a word and watch tasks filter in real time. You planned it, refined it, and Claude built exactly what you approved. The 30 seconds you spent reviewing the plan saved 10 minutes of undoing a wrong-direction implementation.

Permission modes: controlling what Claude can do

Claude Code has three permission modes that you cycle through with Shift+Tab. Each represents a different trust level:

ModeWhat Claude Can DoWhen to Use
DefaultAsks permission for every tool callLearning phase, unfamiliar codebases, sensitive operations
Auto-accept EditsAutomatically approves file reads and editsActive implementation when you trust the direction
Plan ModeRead-only — no edits, no commandsBefore starting any significant task

The important design principle here is that Claude Code is fail-closed. If a tool call does not match any permission rule, it is blocked by default. You have to explicitly grant permission, not explicitly deny it. This means the system errs on the side of caution — unexpected operations require your approval.

In the Configuration section, we will go deeper into the permission model — how to configure allow/deny rules in settings.json, how to set project-level defaults, and how to create fine-grained permission profiles for different workflows. For now, the key takeaway is: you have control. Claude cannot do anything you have not authorized.

Models, Sessions, and Power Features

Model selection

Claude Code defaults to Sonnet — the best balance of speed, quality, and cost for most tasks. You can switch models mid-session with /model:

ModelWhen to Use
Sonnet (default)Day-to-day coding, refactoring, tests — most tasks
OpusSystem design, complex debugging, subtle cross-file bugs
HaikuQuick questions, file exploration, trivial edits

A practical pattern: start with Sonnet, switch to Opus when you hit a genuinely hard problem, then switch back when the hard thinking is done.

Extended thinking

For problems that require multi-step reasoning — debugging concurrency issues, designing API surfaces, untangling circular dependencies — Claude Code gives you two dials.

Per-prompt keywords. Include think carefully, think hard, or ultrathink in a single prompt. Claude gets a private scratchpad to reason through that one problem before responding. Use it when a specific task genuinely benefits from deeper reasoning, not as a default.

Session-wide reasoning effort. Open the /model picker — below the model list you will see a reasoning effort selector (low / medium / high). This sets the default thinking budget for every prompt in the session until you change it. Useful when you are entering a sustained hard-thinking phase (system design, gnarly debugging) and don't want to retype a keyword every time.

The two compose: high effort + ultrathink in a prompt gives maximum thinking depth; low effort with no keyword keeps things snappy. Crank effort up when you need it, crank it back down when you are back to routine edits — higher effort costs more tokens and wall-clock time per response.

Session management

CommandWhat It Does
claude --continueResume the most recent session
claude --resumeInteractive session picker — choose from recent sessions
claude -n "feature-auth"Start a named session — organize parallel workstreams

Two escape sequences to memorize: Esc (once) interrupts Claude mid-action and returns to the prompt. Esc-Esc (twice) rewinds to the state before the last action, undoing any file changes. Think of single-Esc as "stop" and double-Esc as "undo."

Power features: @ references and image input

The @ symbol lets you reference files inline in your prompts. Instead of saying "look at the logger middleware," type @src/middleware/logger.js and Claude reads it before processing your message. You can use multiple @ references in one prompt — "Compare @src/routes/tasks.js with @src/routes/users.js and make the error handling consistent".

Image input lets you paste or drag screenshots, diagrams, and mockups directly into your prompt. Claude analyzes the visual content and can act on it — implementing a UI from a mockup, debugging a visual issue from a screenshot, or following an architecture diagram.

title: Best Practices (Optional)
bodyHtml:
The rules below are not theoretical best practices. They are distilled from hundreds of hours of production use by engineering teams working with Claude Code daily. Every rule exists because someone learned it the hard way. Internalizing these from day one will save you significant time and frustration.

Rule 01: Never Blindly Accept

Claude proposes. You approve. You are always responsible for what enters your codebase.

It is tempting to develop a rhythm of accepting every suggestion — especially when Claude is on a roll and producing good output. But research consistently shows this is dangerous. An ACM study on AI-assisted coding found that developers who accepted all suggestions without review introduced 1.75 times more logic errors than those who reviewed each change.

Claude is highly capable, but it is not infallible. It can misunderstand intent, make incorrect assumptions about your codebase, or generate code that works in isolation but breaks integration points. Your review is the quality gate. The speed gain from skipping review is always less than the time cost of debugging the mistakes.

Rule 02: Context Is Everything

We covered this in the context window section, but it bears repeating as a rule: monitor your context usage and compact proactively.

Watch the Ctx(u) indicator in your statusline. When it hits 70%, run /compact. When it hits 85%, start a fresh session — but do not just quit. Write a handoff note first so the new session can pick up exactly where you left off.

A handoff is how you transfer knowledge between sessions. Before ending a session, ask Claude to summarize the current state — what was accomplished, what is left to do, what decisions were made, and any gotchas the next session should know about. Paste that summary into the new session's first message. This gives fresh Claude full context in a fraction of the token cost.

TRY IT: Practice a session handoff

Pretend your context is nearly full and you need to hand off to a fresh session. You will ask Claude to write a handoff note, then start a new session using it.

Step 1 — Generate handoff note: Ask Claude to write a handoff summary of everything you have done in this session and save it to a file:

Write a handoff note summarizing what we have worked on, what files
were changed, what decisions were made, and what remains to be done.
Save it to HANDOFF.md.

Observe: Claude produces a structured summary — changes made, current state, open items — and saves it to HANDOFF.md. This is your session's knowledge compressed into a few hundred tokens.

Step 2 — Reset the session: Now start a completely fresh session:

1
/clear

Step 3 — Resume with handoff: Ask Claude to read the handoff file and continue from where you left off:

Read HANDOFF.md and pick up where we left off. What should we
work on next?

Observe: Claude reads the file, understands the full context of the previous session, and makes informed suggestions about next steps. A fresh context budget, with the critical knowledge preserved in a few hundred tokens instead of thousands.

Step 4 — Alternative: @ reference: An even faster approach: use an @ reference to inject the file directly into your message, skipping the tool call entirely:

@HANDOFF.md Continue from where we left off.

Observe: The @ syntax injects the file content directly into the prompt — no Read tool call needed. Claude sees it immediately. This is the fastest way to resume from a handoff. A 200-token handoff note replaces thousands of tokens of accumulated conversation.

Rule 03: Test First, Always

Write the failing test before the implementation. This is good engineering practice regardless of AI, but it becomes critical with Claude Code because AI amplifies both good process and bad process equally.

When you start with a test, Claude has a clear, machine-verifiable definition of done. It will write implementation code, run the test, see it fail or pass, and iterate until the test passes. The feedback loop is tight and objective.

When you start with implementation, Claude has only your prose description of what "done" looks like. You end up playing human test suite — reading through code, mentally simulating execution, catching bugs through review alone. This is slower and less reliable.

TRY IT: Test-first in action

Compare two ways of requesting the same feature. One has no test. The other leads with the test definition.

Step 1 — Implementation first — don't do this: This is the implementation-first approach — do NOT paste this:

Add a PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign endpoint that assigns a task to a user

Step 2 — Test-first prompt: Instead, lead with the test — tell Claude what success looks like before writing any code:

Write a test for a PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign endpoint: it should set
assignedTo on the task, return 404 for invalid task IDs, and return
400 if the user ID doesn't exist. Then implement the endpoint to
make the tests pass.

Observe: Claude writes the test first, then the implementation, then runs the test. If it fails, Claude iterates automatically until green. With a test, Claude has a concrete finish line. This is why "write a test that verifies X, then implement X" is the single most effective prompt pattern.

Rule 04: You Are the CPU Scheduler

Your role in the Claude Code workflow is not to write code. It is to orchestrate work. You are the CPU scheduler — you decide what gets processed, in what order, with what priority. Claude is the execution engine that carries out your decisions.

This means your most valuable skills are: decomposing large tasks into well-scoped units of work, providing clear context and intent for each unit, reviewing output for correctness and alignment with the broader system, and making architectural decisions that Claude cannot make because they require business context or taste.

bodyHtml: Configure Claude Code for team-wide consistency — settings hierarchies, memory infrastructure, and your project's AI personality.

title: CLAUDE.md
bodyHtml:
An unconfigured Claude Code session is like hiring a brilliant engineer and giving them no onboarding — tremendous capability, zero project context. Without configuration, you spend 15-30% of every session re-explaining your project structure, coding style, and conventions. As Boris Cherny, engineering lead for Claude Code at Anthropic, puts it: "You should never have to correct Claude twice for the same mistake."

CLAUDE.md is the single most important configuration mechanism in Claude Code. It is a plain markdown file that Claude reads automatically at the start of every session. Whatever you put in this file becomes part of Claude's working knowledge.

The four-tier hierarchy

Claude Code supports CLAUDE.md files at four levels, each with a different scope. See the official memory docs  for the full specification.

TierLocationPurposeGit
Managed (org-wide)macOS: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md Linux / WSL: /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md Windows: C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.mdOrganization-wide policy that applies to every user on the machine. Deployed via MDM, Group Policy, or Ansible. Typical use: company coding standards, security policies, compliance reminders. Cannot be excluded by individual settings.Managed by IT/DevOps
Global~/.claude/CLAUDE.mdYour personal preferences across all projects. Coding style, commit format, response preferences.Not in any repo
ProjectCLAUDE.md (repo root)Team-shared standards. Architecture, commands, conventions. Every developer who clones the repo gets the same instructions. This is where 90% of the value lives.Committed
LocalCLAUDE.local.md (repo root)Personal overrides scoped to this project only. Rare — use when your local setup differs from the team default.Gitignored

More specific wins: if your global CLAUDE.md says "use tabs" but the project CLAUDE.md says "use 2-space indentation," the project rule wins. Most teams only ever use the Global and Project tiers; the Managed tier appears mainly in enterprise deployments.

What goes in each tier

Global

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — just your personal preferences. Typically 2-5 lines:

- Use conventional commits format (feat:, fix:, chore:)
- Prefer verbose explanations over brevity

Local

CLAUDE.local.md at the repo root — machine-specific overrides. Most developers never need this. Use it when your setup differs from the team (e.g., "My local API runs on port 4000 because 3000 is taken"). Add it to .gitignore so it stays off the repo.

Project

CLAUDE.md at repo root — this is the important one. A well-structured project CLAUDE.md has four sections:

Commands — The highest-value section. Saves Claude from reading package.json and CI configs every session.

1

## Commands

npm run dev        # run the server on port 3000 with auto-restart on file changes (default)
npm start          # run the server on port 3000 without --watch (one-shot)

No test runner or linter configured.
API routes require header: x-api-key: taskflow-dev-key

Architecture — How the codebase is organized. Prevents Claude from exploring the directory tree every session.

1
2

## Architecture
Express.js REST API. Entry point: src/server.js
Request flow: cors → json → static → logger → auth → routes

Key layers:
- src/middleware/auth.js   — API key check
- src/routes/tasks.js      — CRUD for /api/tasks
- src/routes/users.js      — CRUD for /api/users
- src/data/store.js        — reads/writes JSON files synchronously
- src/utils/helpers.js     — generateId(prefix), timestamp()

Data Model — Entity names and fields. Prevents Claude from hallucinating schema fields that do not exist.

1
2
3
## Data Model
Tasks: id, title, description, status, priority, assignee, tags
Users: id, name, email, role

Intentional Decisions — The section most teams miss. Without it, Claude will "fix" things that look wrong but are deliberate.

1
2

4
5
## Intentional Design Decisions
- JSON file storage (not a database) — intentional for simplicity
- Synchronous file reads in store.js — acceptable for single-user dev server
- No test framework configured — tests are added as a workshop exercise
- Hardcoded API key in auth.js — development only, not a security oversight

Growing your CLAUDE.md over time

Your first CLAUDE.md should be 10-20 lines — just the essentials. Then let it grow from real usage: (1) Claude makes a mistake, (2) you correct it, (3) you add a rule to CLAUDE.md so it never happens again. After two weeks of active development, your CLAUDE.md will contain exactly the rules that matter — every one earned from a real correction, no speculative bloat.

The /memory command adds notes to your CLAUDE.md automatically. When Claude makes a mistake, fix it and say: "Remember: always use our custom logger instead of console.log." Claude encodes this into your project memory.

Keep it under 200 lines: CLAUDE.md files are loaded in full at session start — there is no hard cutoff. But the official guidance is to target under 200 lines per file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence. If your instructions are growing large, split them using .claude/rules/ files with path scoping (covered in the Rules section).

TRY IT: Build your CLAUDE.md hierarchy

Use /init to generate the project-level CLAUDE.md, then create the global tier with your personal preferences.

Step 1 — Auto-generate project CLAUDE.md: Generate the project-level CLAUDE.md automatically. Claude will analyze the codebase and produce a first draft:

Tell Claude:

/init

Observe: Claude scans package.json, source files, and project structure, then writes a CLAUDE.md with commands, architecture, and conventions it discovered. Review the output — this is a solid starting point that you can refine over time.

Step 2 — Exit Claude Code: Exit the Claude Code session so you can work in the terminal:

Tell Claude:

/exit

Step 3 — Create global tier: Create a global CLAUDE.md with your personal preferences (applies to all your projects on this machine):

Run in terminal:

1
2

mkdir -p ~/.claude && cat > ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md << 'EOF'

- Use conventional commits format (feat:, fix:, chore:)
- This is a learning environment — prefer verbose explanations over brevity
EOF

Observe: This file now exists at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and will be loaded for every Claude Code session on this machine, regardless of which project you are in.

Step 4 — Launch Claude Code: Start a new session and verify both tiers load:

Run in terminal:

1
claude

Step 5 — Verify the hierarchy: Ask Claude what it knows:

Tell Claude:

What do you know about this project from your CLAUDE.md files? List the instructions you received from each tier.

Observe: Claude should describe instructions from both tiers — your global preferences and the project conventions from /init. This is the complete picture Claude starts every session with.

The .claude/ directory

CLAUDE.md is not the only configuration file. The .claude/ directory at your project root is the complete extension system — settings, agents, commands, hooks, and rules. Everything is committed to git except personal files, so new developers get the full AI configuration on clone.

<repo root>/
├── CLAUDE.md                   # Project instructions              ← committed   (this section)
├── CLAUDE.local.md             # Personal overrides                ← gitignored
├── .mcp.json                   # MCP server configuration          ← committed   (Extensions: MCP)
└── .claude/
    ├── settings.json           # Permissions & config              ← committed   (Settings section)
    ├── settings.local.json     # Personal settings                 ← gitignored
    ├── rules/                  # Path-scoped instructions          ← committed   (Rules section)
    ├── agents/                 # Specialist sub-agent definitions  ← committed   (Extensions)
    ├── skills/                 # Reusable slash commands           ← committed   (Extensions)
    └── hooks/                  # Lifecycle automation scripts      ← committed   (Extensions)

We will build this directory out piece by piece over the next sections.

title: Settings
bodyHtml:
While CLAUDE.md controls what Claude knows, settings.json controls what Claude can do. It defines permissions, behavioral defaults, and registers extension points like hooks and MCP servers. It is the difference between giving Claude instructions and giving Claude guardrails.

The permission model

The permissions key is the heart of settings.json. Each rule is a string in the format Tool(specifier) where Tool is the tool name and specifier is a glob pattern:

Permission rule syntax

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Read(**)",           // Read any file
      "Edit(src/**)",       // Edit files in src/
      "Bash(npm test*)",    // Run npm test commands
      "Bash(git status)",   // Run git status
      "Bash(git diff*)"     // Run git diff variants
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Edit(.env*)",        // Never edit .env files
      "Read(.env*)",        // Never read .env files
      "Bash(rm -rf*)",      // Block destructive commands
      "Bash(git push*)"     // Prevent accidental pushes
    ]
  }
}

Deny rules always take priority over allow rules. If you allow Read(**) but deny Read(.env*), the .env files are blocked even though the wildcard would match them. Deny is absolute.

allow / ask / deny

LevelBehavior
allowExplicitly permitted. Claude proceeds without asking. Use for safe, routine operations the team trusts.
ask (default)Not in allow or deny. Claude stops and asks for permission. This is the safe default for unknown operations.
denyExplicitly blocked. Claude cannot proceed even if the user approves. Use for security-critical protections.

Security property: The permission model is fail-closed by default. If a tool call does not match any allow rule, Claude stops and asks. It never silently proceeds.

    ],

Step 3 — Create .env: Create a dummy .env file so we can test the deny rule:

Step 5 — Test allowed operation: Ask Claude to edit a source file:

Observe: Claude reads and edits the file without asking permission — it matches both Read() and Edit(src/).

Step 6 — Test denied operation: Now test a denied operation:

Tell Claude:

Can you add a timestamp to .env?

Observe: Claude refuses — it cannot read or edit .env files because of the deny rule in settings.json. This is not a suggestion Claude can override; it is a hard guardrail enforced by the platform. Your team's secrets are protected by configuration, not by hoping Claude follows instructions.

Settings.json is your security boundary. The deny list is a hard wall — Claude cannot bypass it even if the user explicitly asks. This is how you enforce enterprise security policies.

Settings scopes and precedence

Like CLAUDE.md, settings files exist at multiple scopes:

ScopeLocationShared?
User~/.claude/settings.jsonNo — personal, all projects
Project.claude/settings.jsonYes — committed to git
Local.claude/settings.local.jsonNo — gitignored, this project only

When the same setting appears at multiple levels, the more specific scope wins: local overrides project, project overrides user. Enterprise administrators also have a managed policy scope that sits above all three and cannot be overridden.

Tip: Run /config inside Claude Code to open the visual settings editor. It shows all active settings, their sources, and lets you modify them without editing JSON.

Practical permission patterns

Here are permission patterns that work well for different team scenarios:

PatternRulesUse Case
Read-mostlyallow: Read(), Edit(src/), deny: .env*Junior devs, code review, exploration sessions
Full developmentallow: Read(), Edit(), Bash(npm*), Bash(git*)Active development with safe command set
Locked downallow: Read(src/**), deny: everything elseSecurity audits, compliance reviews
CI/CD integrationallow: Bash(npm test*), Bash(npm run build)Automated pipeline contexts

What else lives in settings.json

Beyond permissions, settings.json has keys for other major systems that we cover in the Extensions section:

KeyPurposeCovered in
hooksScripts that fire at lifecycle events (auto-test after edits, block dangerous commands)Extensions: Hooks
envEnvironment variables applied to every sessionThis workshop
modelOverride the default model for this projectThis workshop

Note: MCP servers are configured in .mcp.json at the project root, not in settings.json. See the Extensions: MCP section for details.

title: Rules
bodyHtml:
CLAUDE.md gives Claude project-wide context that loads on every session. But what about instructions that only matter in specific contexts? You do not want Claude thinking about your database migration conventions when it is editing a React component. You do not want your testing rules consuming context when Claude is working on deployment scripts.

The .claude/rules/ directory solves this. It contains markdown files with optional YAML frontmatter that specifies when each rule should activate. Rules only load into context when Claude is working on files that match their scope — keeping your context budget clean and your instructions relevant.

How rules work

Each file in .claude/rules/ is a markdown file. Without frontmatter, it loads on every session (equivalent to putting the content in CLAUDE.md). With a globs frontmatter field, it only loads when Claude is working on files matching those patterns:

.claude/rules/testing.md — loads only for test files

---
globs:
  - "**/*.test.js"
  - "**/*.test.ts"
  - "**/*.spec.js"
  - "**/*.spec.ts"
---

# Testing Standards

- Use describe/it blocks, not test() directly
- Each test file tests exactly one module
- Mock external dependencies, never real HTTP calls
- Test names follow: "should [expected behavior] when [condition]"
- Always include at least one edge case test per function

When Claude opens or edits a file matching **/*.test.js, this rule automatically loads into context. When Claude is editing a route handler, this rule stays out of the context window — saving tokens and preventing irrelevant instructions from confusing the model.

.claude/rules/api-routes.md — loads only for route files

---
globs:
  - "src/routes/**"
---

# API Route Conventions

- Every route handler must validate input before processing
- Use the project's standard error format: { error: string }
- Return 201 for creation, 204 for deletion, 200 for everything else
- Never access the data store directly — use functions from store.js
- Log all errors with the request method and path

Rules vs. CLAUDE.md: when to use which

The decision is straightforward:

Use CLAUDE.md When...Use .claude/rules/ When...
The instruction applies to every sessionThe instruction only applies to certain files
It's a project-wide convention (naming, architecture)It's a domain-specific convention (tests, routes, migrations)
It's a key command (test, build, deploy)Loading it for every session wastes context
It's critical enough to always be in contextDifferent file types have different standards
It's fewer than 5 lines of instructionIt's detailed enough to justify its own file

A good heuristic: if you find yourself writing a section in CLAUDE.md that starts with "When editing test files..." or "For files in src/routes/...", that section should be a rule file instead. The globs frontmatter does the conditional logic for you, and your CLAUDE.md stays lean.

Rules are committed to git just like CLAUDE.md, so the entire team gets the same path-scoped instructions automatically. When a senior engineer adds a new rule for database migration files, every developer benefits from it on their next pull.

Building a rules library

A well-configured project might have 3-5 rule files covering the major domains:

  • testing.md — conventions for test files (describe/it structure, mocking, assertions)
  • api-routes.md — conventions for route handlers (validation, error format, status codes)
  • database.md — conventions for data access (query patterns, migration standards)
  • components.md — conventions for UI components (naming, props, state management)
  • security.md — security-critical rules (input sanitization, auth checks, secrets handling)

Path-scoped rules keep your context efficient. Instead of loading all domain knowledge on every session, Claude only receives the rules relevant to the files it is currently touching.

title: Auto Memory
bodyHtml:
You have learned to write CLAUDE.md manually — carefully crafting instructions from real corrections. But Claude Code also has an automatic memory system that lets it learn from your sessions without you writing configuration files by hand. This section covers three tools: auto memory (Claude's own notes), the /memory command (browsing and editing memory), and /init (project bootstrapping).

Together with CLAUDE.md, these form a feedback loop where Claude learns your preferences and project patterns over time.

Auto memory: Claude takes its own notes

Auto memory lets Claude accumulate knowledge across sessions without you writing anything. As you work, Claude decides what is worth remembering — build commands, debugging insights, architecture notes, code style preferences — and may save notes for its future self. It does not save every session; saving is a judgement call Claude makes based on whether the information would help future conversations.

Version requirement

Auto memory requires Claude Code v2.1.59 or later. Run claude --version to check. On older versions this chapter's TRY IT will silently do nothing.

CLAUDE.md (You Write)Auto Memory (Claude Writes)
You author it explicitlyClaude saves it from session learnings
Project architecture, commands, conventionsBuild commands, debugging insights, preferences
Committed to git — shared with teamMachine-local — not in project repo
Loaded in full at session startFirst 200 lines (or 25KB) of MEMORY.md loaded at session start
Your instructions to ClaudeClaude's notes to its future self

When you correct Claude during a session — "no, we use Vitest not Jest" or "always add the logger import when creating route files" — Claude can auto-save that correction so it does not make the same mistake next time. You can also ask Claude to remember something explicitly: "remember that the API tests require a local Redis instance." Whether Claude actually writes depends on how save-worthy the note looks to it. A more forceful nudge — "add this to auto memory now" — reliably triggers a save.

Auto memory is stored outside your project repo at ~/.claude/projects//memory/. The directory contains a MEMORY.md index file and optional topic files for detailed notes:

Auto memory directory structure

~/
└── .claude/
    └── projects/
        └── <project>/
            └── memory/
                ├── MEMORY.md           # Concise index (first 200 lines / 25KB loaded every session)
                ├── debugging.md        # Detailed notes on debugging patterns
                ├── api-conventions.md  # API design decisions Claude discovered
                └── ...                 # Any other topic files Claude creates

All worktrees and subdirectories within the same git repository share one auto memory directory. The files are plain markdown — you can read, edit, or delete them at any time.

Only MEMORY.md is loaded at session start — and only its first 200 lines (or 25 KB, whichever comes first). Topic files like debugging.md or api-conventions.md are not in context by default; Claude reads them on demand using its normal file tools when it needs them. That is why Claude keeps MEMORY.md as a concise index and moves detailed notes into topic files — it keeps startup context small while preserving access to deeper notes.

Think of CLAUDE.md as the employee handbook you write for Claude, and auto memory as Claude's personal notebook where it writes down things it learned on the job. Both are read at the start of every session. Both make Claude smarter over time. But CLAUDE.md is your authoring, and auto memory is Claude's.

The /memory command: browse and edit

The /memory command is a browser and editor for Claude's memory sources. When you run /memory, it lists every CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, and .claude/rules/ file loaded in your current session, plus a single "Open auto-memory folder" entry at the bottom. Auto-memory files are not expanded inline — that entry is a link that opens the auto-memory directory in your editor when you select it. The command also lets you toggle auto memory on or off.

Select any file from the list to open it in your editor. This is useful for:

  • Inspecting what auto memory has saved — select "Open auto-memory folder" to browse
  • Editing your project CLAUDE.md without leaving the session
  • Reviewing which .claude/rules/ files are active
  • Verifying your user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is loaded

To add instructions to CLAUDE.md, either edit the file directly via /memory or ask Claude explicitly: "add this to CLAUDE.md." To let Claude handle it automatically, just correct Claude during a session and it may save the lesson to auto memory on its own.

/init: bootstrapping a new project

The /init command is the fastest way to go from zero configuration to a working CLAUDE.md. When you run /init in a project that has no CLAUDE.md, Claude analyzes your project — reading package.json, scanning the source tree, examining test configurations, checking for linters and formatters — and generates a first-draft CLAUDE.md based on what it discovers.

This is not a magic bullet — the generated file is a starting point, not a finished product. But it is a significantly better starting point than a blank file, and it demonstrates what kind of information belongs in CLAUDE.md:

  • Project overview (language, framework, purpose)
  • Key commands (test, build, lint, start)
  • File structure with brief descriptions
  • Detected conventions (ESM vs CJS, semicolons, indentation)
  • Dependencies and their roles

The best workflow for a new project: run /init, review the output, trim anything Claude already knows from training data (no need to explain what Express is), add project-specific context Claude could not infer (deployment targets, team conventions, current sprint), and commit. You go from zero to a useful CLAUDE.md in about 3 minutes.

Managed policy and CLAUDE.md exclusions

In enterprise environments, administrators can deploy a managed policy CLAUDE.md to a system-level path on every developer machine. This is the highest priority tier — it cannot be overridden or excluded by individual developers. It is how organizations enforce universal standards: security baselines, compliance requirements, approved tool lists.

Managed policy file locations

# macOS
/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md

# Linux / WSL
/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md

# Windows
C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md

Deploy this file using your configuration management system — MDM, Group Policy, Ansible, Chef, or similar tools. It does not live in the project repo and developers cannot edit it.

The claudeMdExcludes setting (still named as the JSON key) lets you prevent specific CLAUDE.md files from being loaded. Patterns match against absolute file paths using glob syntax. This is useful in monorepos where nested CLAUDE.md files from other teams or vendored code might conflict with your top-level configuration:

Excluding nested CLAUDE.md files

// In .claude/settings.json
{
  "claudeMdExcludes": [
    "**/vendor/**/CLAUDE.md",
    "**/third_party/**/CLAUDE.md",
    "**/node_modules/**/CLAUDE.md"
  ]
}

Without this exclusion, a CLAUDE.md file buried in a vendor dependency could inject unexpected instructions into your Claude sessions. Managed policy CLAUDE.md files cannot be excluded — organization-wide instructions always apply.

The complete memory architecture

Putting it all together, Claude Code's memory system has six layers that compose at session start:

LayerSourceAuthorshipScopeLocation
Managed PolicySystem-level CLAUDE.mdIT/Security teamOrganization-wideSystem path (deployed via MDM/Ansible)
User CLAUDE.md~/.claude/CLAUDE.mdDeveloperAll projects on this machineHome directory
Project CLAUDE.md./CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.mdTeamThis projectProject repo (committed)
Local CLAUDE.md./CLAUDE.local.mdDeveloperThis project, this machineProject repo (gitignored)
Auto Memory~/.claude/projects//memory/ClaudeThis project, this machineHome directory (machine-local)
.claude/rules/Path-scoped markdown filesTeamFile-pattern-specificProject repo (committed)

All layers merge into Claude's working context at session start. The total token cost is the sum of all loaded content — which is why keeping each layer lean and focused matters. A well-architected memory system gives Claude deep project knowledge at minimal context cost.

TRY IT: Teach Claude something and verify it persists

Correct Claude during a session so it auto-saves a learning, then verify it remembers in a fresh session. Use /memory to browse what was saved.

Step 1 — Start Claude Code:

Run in terminal:

1
claude

Step 2 — Teach Claude: Tell Claude to remember a project fact:

Tell Claude:

Remember this for future sessions: this project uses
synchronous file I/O in store.js. Never suggest async
fs methods — the sync approach is intentional. Add this
to auto memory now.

Observe: Claude acknowledges and writes to auto memory. You should see a "Writing memory" line in the output. If you don't, auto-save is a judgement call — Claude decides per note whether it's worth keeping. The explicit "add this to auto memory now" nudge in the prompt above makes the save reliable; if you leave it off, Claude may skip the save and you'll see nothing written.

Step 3 — Browse memory: Open the memory browser:

Tell Claude:

/memory

Observe: You see a numbered list — typically your User memory (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), Project memory (./CLAUDE.md), any .claude/rules/ files, and a final entry labeled "Open auto-memory folder". The first entries show the CLAUDE.md and rules files loaded at session start; they are not where auto memory lives. To see what Claude saved, arrow down to "Open auto-memory folder" and press Enter — it opens ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ in your editor. Inside, look at MEMORY.md and any topic files. You should find the note about synchronous file I/O that Claude just saved.

Alternative — peek from the shell without leaving Claude Code:

Tell Claude:

! ls ~/.claude/projects/*/memory/ && cat ~/.claude/projects/*/memory/MEMORY.md

Observe: You see the memory directory contents and the current MEMORY.md index. This is the same file /memory opens in your editor.

Step 4 — Verify persistence: Prove the memory survives a fresh session. First exit:

Tell Claude:

/exit

Then restart Claude Code:

Run in terminal:

1
claude

Now ask about the thing you taught it, without re-explaining:

Tell Claude:

How does this project handle file I/O in store.js? Should I use async or sync methods?

Observe: Claude answers with the sync-is-intentional guidance from the previous session — even though the conversation history is gone. The memory was loaded from MEMORY.md at session start and is part of Claude's working context.

Auto memory turns corrections into persistent knowledge without you editing any files. Claude saves what it learns, /memory is your dashboard for browsing the whole memory stack, and the auto memory folder itself is plain markdown you can inspect or edit directly.

title: Claude Code Extensions
bodyHtml:
The extension system provides four core systems that transform Claude Code from a single-session assistant into a programmable AI operating system:

IconSystemDescription
🤖AgentsSub-agents with isolated context windows. Expert-prompted for specific domains like code review, security audit, or test generation.
📚SkillsDirectory-based packages in .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md entrypoint. User-invocable via slash commands or auto-discovered by context.
⚡HooksScripts, HTTP endpoints, prompts, or agent handlers triggered at lifecycle events. Cannot be overridden by prompts — structural enforcement.
🔌MCPModel Context Protocol — the standard interface connecting Claude to external services like GitHub, Jira, and Slack.

Each system can operate independently, but the real power emerges when they compose. Everything in .claude/ is git-controlled — when a new team member clones the repo, they inherit the full extension system on first clone.

This section covers each system in depth, starting with skills.

title: Skills
bodyHtml:
Skills are the unified extension system in Claude Code, following the open Agent Skills standard (agentskills.io). They replace the older "commands" system and serve a dual purpose: they are both reusable knowledge patterns that Claude auto-discovers when relevant, and user-invocable slash commands that developers trigger explicitly with /<name>. A single skill can serve both roles, or specialize in one.

Each skill lives in a directory under .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md entrypoint file. The directory-based structure is intentional — a skill can bundle supporting files (templates, schemas, reference docs) alongside its instructions, keeping everything self-contained and portable.

Bundled skills

Claude Code ships with five bundled skills that are available in every project without any configuration:

IconSkillDescription
📦/batchProcess multiple files or operations in a single pass.
🔌/claude-apiGenerate code that calls the Anthropic API.
🐛/debugSystematic debugging workflow with root cause analysis.
🔄/loopIterative refinement loop — repeat until quality criteria met.
✂️/simplifyReduce complexity — fewer lines, clearer logic, less indirection.

These bundled skills demonstrate the patterns you should follow when building your own. They use frontmatter fields, $ARGUMENTS substitution, and context forking — all features available to custom skills.

Skill file format

A SKILL.md file has YAML frontmatter that controls how and when the skill activates, followed by markdown instructions that Claude follows when the skill is invoked:

.claude/skills/tdd-workflow/SKILL.md

---
name: tdd-workflow
description: "Test-Driven Development workflow: Red → Green → Refactor"
user-invocable: true
argument-hint: "<file-path>"
allowed-tools:
  - Read
  - Edit
  - Write
  - Bash
---

Follow the TDD workflow strictly:

## Step 1: Red
Write a failing test first. Run it to confirm it fails.
Command: `npm test -- --testPathPattern=$ARGUMENTS`

## Step 2: Green
Write the minimum code to make the test pass. No more.

## Step 3: Refactor
Clean up both test and implementation. Run tests again.

## Rules
- NEVER write implementation before the test exists
- Each test should test ONE behavior
- Test file must exist before source file

Key frontmatter fields control the skill's behavior:

FieldPurposeExample
nameSkill identifier (used as /name for slash commands)tdd-workflow
descriptionWhen to trigger — Claude uses this for auto-discovery"TDD workflow for test-first development"
user-invocableIf true, appears as a slash command (/tdd-workflow)true | false
argument-hintHint text shown after /name in autocomplete"<file-path>"
allowed-toolsRestrict which tools the skill can use[Read, Edit, Bash]
modelOverride the model for this skill executionhaiku, sonnet, opus
context: forkRun the skill in an isolated context (like a sub-agent)fork
disable-model-invocationIf true, skill only provides context — no AI reasoningtrue
$ARGUMENTS / $1 $2Special variables — replaced with user input after /name"src/routes/tasks.js"

Two activation modes

Skills activate in two distinct ways, and understanding the difference is key to designing effective skills:

Auto-Discovered (Passive)User-Invoked (Active)
Claude reads the skill's description fieldDeveloper types /skill-name to trigger explicitly
When working context matches, skill loads automaticallyuser-invocable: true must be set in frontmatter
No user action required — seamless$ARGUMENTS captures text after the command name
Good for: conventions, standards, patternsGood for: workflows, multi-step processes, reports
Example: OWASP checklist loads when editing auth codeExample: /tdd-workflow src/routes/tasks.js

Many skills work in both modes. A tdd-workflow skill can auto-discover when Claude notices you are writing tests, and also be explicitly invoked with /tdd-workflow when you want to force the workflow for a specific file.

Dynamic context with !command!

Skills can inject dynamic information into their instructions with the !command! syntax — for example, embedding !git diff --stat! inside a review skill runs the command at skill-load time and substitutes the output inline before Claude reasons over it. This makes skills adaptive to the current project state. Bangs run with your shell permissions and are not sandboxed — only use trusted commands, never user-controlled input.

Skills are packages

Skills are directory-based packages, not just prompt files. The SKILL.md is the entrypoint, but the directory can contain anything the skill needs — scripts, templates, reference documents, schemas, example files:

<repo root>/
└── .claude/
    └── skills/
        └── generate-api/
            ├── SKILL.md              # Entrypoint — instructions + frontmatter
            ├── route-template.js     # Template Claude uses as a starting point
            ├── openapi-schema.yaml   # Reference schema Claude checks against
            ├── validate.sh           # Script invoked via !bash validate.sh!
            └── examples/
                ├── good-route.js     # Well-structured route
                └── bad-route.js      # Anti-pattern for Claude to avoid

Claude can read any file in the skill directory. This means you can package complex workflows — a code generator with templates, a review checklist with reference examples, a migration tool with schema definitions — as self-contained, portable units. Copy the directory to another project and the skill works.

This is what makes skills more powerful than just a well-crafted prompt. A prompt is instructions. A skill is instructions plus reference materials plus scripts plus templates — everything Claude needs to execute a workflow reliably.

Where skills live

Skills can live in three places, and the location determines who gets them:

LocationScopeUse for
.claude/skills/ (repo root)Team-shared, committed to gitProject-specific workflows — /validate-route referencing this API's conventions, /design-review against this project's ADRs
~/.claude/skills/Personal, machine-globalYour individual habits across every project — preferred commit-message style, personal explainer formats
Bundled (ship with Claude Code)Available everywhere, no setupThe five shown at the top of this page — /batch, /claude-api, /debug, /loop, /simplify

Rule of thumb: if another teammate on this repo would want the same slash command, commit it under .claude/skills/. If it is idiosyncratic to how you personally work, put it in ~/.claude/skills/. All TRY IT exercises in this workshop create project-level skills because they reference project-specific standards — making them personal would mean duplicating those standards for every project you touch.

Real-world skill examples

The EPCC Workflow Plugin  is an open-source collection of skills for a full development workflow:

SkillPurpose
/prdGenerate a Product Requirements Document
/trdGenerate a Technical Requirements Document
/epcc-exploreMap the codebase — code archaeologist
/epcc-planDesign an implementation plan
/epcc-codeImplement with auto-validation
/epcc-commitRun tests and commit
/epcc-resumeResume interrupted work

Browse the source — each .md file is a skill you can read to see how production teams structure their workflow prompts. In the SDLC phases of this workshop, you will build your own skills (/validate-spec, /design-review, /self-review) following the same patterns.

Build a skill that validates a specific route file when invoked, demonstrating the $ARGUMENTS variable and dynamic context features.

mkdir -p .claude/skills/validate-route && cat > .claude/skills/validate-route/SKILL.md << 'SKILLEOF'

description: "Validate an API route file against project conventions"

---

Validate the route file: $ARGUMENTS

1. All handlers validate input before processing
2. Error responses use { error: "message" } format
3. Correct HTTP status codes (201 create, 204 delete)

!npm test -- --watchAll=false 2>&1 | tail -5!

Observe: The skill is now available as /validate-route. The $ARGUMENTS variable will be replaced with whatever file path the developer specifies.

Step 2 — Start Claude Code: Start a Claude Code session:

Run in terminal:

Step 3 — Test the skill: Invoke the skill:

Observe: Claude loads the skill, replaces $ARGUMENTS with src/routes/tasks.js, executes the npm test command for dynamic context, and then validates the route file against the listed standards. Skills bridge the gap between reusable conventions (auto-discovered) and team workflows (user-invoked) — the $ARGUMENTS and !command! features make them dynamic and context-aware, far more powerful than static documentation.

Where do standards belong?

You may have noticed that the validate-route skill contains API standards (error format, status codes, store.js usage) that also appear in CLAUDE.md, @imported docs, and .claude/rules/. This overlap is intentional — each location serves a different purpose based on when Claude needs the information:

LocationWhen It LoadsUse ForContext Cost
CLAUDE.md / @importsEvery session, always in contextThings Claude should know no matter what it is doing — project overview, key commands, universal conventionsAlways paid
.claude/rules/ with globsWhen Claude touches matching filesStandards for a category of files — "when editing route files, always validate input"Paid only when relevant files are open
SkillsOnly when invoked or auto-discoveredActive workflows that produce output — "validate this file against our checklist and report findings"Zero until invoked

The key distinction: rules are passive context — Claude knows about them while working on matching files (progressive disclosure). A skill is an active workflow that uses standards to produce a structured output. The validate-route skill is not just "here are our API standards" — it is "run this checklist against a specific file and tell me what is wrong."

The anti-pattern is putting standards only in a skill. Then Claude would not know about them during normal coding — it would only apply them when you explicitly invoke the validation. You want the knowledge ambient (.claude/rules/ with globs) and the workflow on-demand (skills).

title: Custom Agents
bodyHtml:
Foundation → Sub-Agents covered the built-in agent types (Explore, Plan, general-purpose, claude-code-guide, statusline-setup) — the workhorses Claude Code ships with. This page is about writing your own: project-specific specialists like a code-reviewer that knows your standards, a security-auditor for your threat model, a test-writer that matches your framework.

Custom agents use the same isolation mechanics as the built-ins — fresh context window, summary-only return, depth-limited to one level. The difference is authorship. You define them as markdown files in .claude/agents/ and commit them to git, so everyone on the team inherits the same specialists on clone.

SkillsCustom Agents
What they areDirectory-based packages (SKILL.md + templates, scripts, reference files)Single .md file defining a specialist worker
ContextShares your sessionFresh, isolated — cannot see your conversation
Best forReusable workflows, slash commandsDeep analysis, code review, security audit
Invoked byYou type /skill-nameClaude spawns them via the Agent tool
Think of it asA toolkit you use at your deskA specialist contractor you send on a mission

How agent files are structured

An agent file lives in .claude/agents/ and has two parts: YAML frontmatter that configures the agent's behavior (tools, model, permissions), and a markdown body that serves as the agent's system instructions. Let's create one.

Observe: Claude spawns your custom code-reviewer with isolated context — same mechanic Foundation's TRY IT used for parallel Explore agents. The agent reads and reviews the file, then returns a structured summary to your session. The review consumed the agent's context, not yours. This is the payoff of authoring custom agents: a specialist that knows your standards, reusable across every PR, committed to git so the whole team shares it.

Agent frontmatter reference

The agent you just created used name, description, and tools. Here is the full set of frontmatter fields:

FieldPurposeExample
nameDisplay name in logs and parent contextcode-reviewer
descriptionWhen to trigger this agent — helps the Agent tool match context"Triggered for PR reviews"

The key design principle: least privilege. Give each agent only the tools it needs. A code-reviewer needs Read, Glob, Grep — not Write, Edit, or Bash. The isolation mechanics (fresh context, summary-only return, depth=1) work the same way as the built-in sub-agents covered in Foundation.

Advanced agent patterns

PatternHow it worksUse case
Background executionAgent runs in background while you keep working. /agents to list, resume by ID.Long-running reviews, bulk analysis
Persistent memorymemory: project — agent reads/writes shared MEMORY.md across sessions.Recurring audits, cross-session knowledge
Worktree isolationisolation: worktree — agent gets its own git worktree. Edits never conflict with yours.Parallel agents that all edit code, safe prototyping
Agent resume/agents lists all agents. Resume any by ID to check progress or retrieve results.Monitor background agents, get partial results

Building an agent library

A mature project typically has 3–6 agents covering different domains:

Agent FileDescription
code-reviewer.mdSenior Engineer — correctness, patterns, naming, edge cases. Tools: Read, Glob, Grep.
security-auditor.mdAppSec Specialist — OWASP Top 10, injection, auth, secrets. Tools: Read, Glob, Grep.

architecture-reviewer.mdSystems Architect — design patterns, scalability, ADR compliance. Tools: Read, Glob, Grep.

Each agent is committed to git. When a new developer joins the team, they inherit the full agent library on first clone.
