title: TDD with Claude
bodyHtml:
Acceptance Criteria Become Executable Tests

You have a validated spec, an architecture plan, and CLAUDE.md pointing to the active work. Implementation is plan execution — not creative exploration. The approach: convert acceptance criteria into tests BEFORE writing code, then implement to pass them.

Acceptance Criteria → Phase 1 → Generate Tests (Tests fail — nothing exists yet) → Implement (Build to pass the tests) → Tests Pass (Every criterion verified)

This gives Claude two constraints: the spec/architecture (design intent) AND the failing tests (executable expectations). Double verification — and a natural guardrail against over-engineering.

What to Watch During Implementation

SignalHealthyUnhealthy
Test generationTests map 1:1 to acceptance criteriaTests are generic or don't trace to requirements
Exploration phaseClaude reads 3-5 files before planningClaude starts writing code immediately without reading
Pattern matchingPlan follows existing conventionsPlan introduces different patterns than the rest of the project
Scope adherencePlan covers exactly what the spec saysPlan adds extra features 'while I'm at it'
Error formatPlan references the architecture's error formatPlan invents a new error shape
Test resultsTests fail before implementation, pass afterTests pass before implementation (tests are wrong)

Hands-on: Tests First, Then Implement

TRY IT: Generate tests, then implement to pass them

You have all Phase 1 and Phase 2 artifacts in place. Start with a clean context — your artifacts are the context bridge, not chat history.

Step 1: Start fresh context

Clear your conversation history to start fresh for implementation. Your Phase 2 artifacts (spec, architecture plan, CLAUDE.md) are already in files — you don't need the chat history from previous phases:

Run in terminal:

1
/clear

Observe: Context is cleared. Claude will re-read CLAUDE.md automatically, which now points to the active work (spec, architecture plan). All your Phase 1 and 2 artifacts are in files — nothing was lost. This is why we write decisions to files, not chat.

Step 2: Generate tests from acceptance criteria

First, generate tests from your acceptance criteria. No implementation yet — just the tests:

Tell Claude:

Read the acceptance criteria and API contract in
docs/specs/task-comments.md.

Write tests that verify EVERY acceptance criterion:
- Positive tests (valid input accepted)
- Negative tests (invalid input rejected, missing fields, non-existent tasks)
- Assert the API contract exactly (status codes, response shape, error format)
- Verify behavior matches docs/architecture/task-comments.md

Follow the project's existing test structure. If none exists,
use the ecosystem default.
Do not implement anything yet — only write the tests.

Observe: Claude reads the validated spec and generates test cases that map to each criterion. Check: does every acceptance criterion have at least one test? Are the assertions specific (checking status codes, error format, field names) rather than vague? The spec is the build contract — not the raw stories from Phase 1 — because validate-spec tightened its criteria and added the API contract the tests need to assert against.

Step 3: Confirm red — all tests fail

Run the tests. Every single one should fail — that is the point:

Tell Claude:

Run the tests.

Observe: Every test fails. This is the 'red' in red-green-refactor. Check three things: (1) the test runner found all test files — no configuration issues, (2) every test fails because the feature is not implemented, not because of syntax errors or import problems, (3) count the tests — this is your progress meter for the implementation phase.

Step 4: Claude writes implementation plan

Now ask Claude to write an implementation plan scoped to the full spec, not just the tests:

Tell Claude:

Now implement the ACTIVE unit. Every acceptance criterion in the
spec must be implemented — including [UI] criteria that aren't
covered by automated tests. The tests are a subset of the contract,
not the whole contract.

Read these artifacts first:
- Feature spec: docs/specs/task-comments.md
- Architecture: docs/architecture/task-comments.md

Before writing any code:
1. Write an implementation plan to docs/plans/task-comments.md
   with checkboxes for each step
2. Flag any decisions where you need my input (mark with QUESTION:)

Do not implement yet — just write the plan for my review.

Observe: Claude reads the spec, architecture, and existing code, then writes an implementation plan. Review the plan: does the file order make sense? Does it cover every acceptance criterion — including the [UI] ones that don't have tests? Are there scope creep items to remove?

Step 5: Resolve open questions

If the plan has QUESTION: markers, ask Claude to resolve them with its best recommendation rather than leaving them as open questions for you:

Tell Claude:

For each QUESTION in the plan, replace it with your
best recommendation based on the spec and architecture.
Explain your reasoning briefly inline.
Update the plan file.

Observe: Claude replaces each QUESTION with a concrete recommendation and a one-line rationale. Now you review a complete plan with proposed answers, not a plan with blanks to fill. Much easier to approve or override a recommendation than to answer from scratch.

Step 6: Handoff and execute

Open docs/plans/task-comments.md in your editor. Review it, then hand it back:

Tell Claude:

I reviewed the plan in docs/plans/task-comments.md.
Follow it as specified. Implement one step at a time,
mark each checkbox as done. When all steps are complete,
run the tests.

Observe: Claude implements step by step, running tests periodically. Watch the test count: 0/N passing at start, then climbing as each piece lands. When all tests pass, implementation is complete. Check that error responses match the architecture's error format.

Step 7: Verify traceability

Verify all tests pass and check traceability:

Tell Claude:

Run all tests. For each acceptance criterion on the task
comments stories in requirements/stories.md, point to the
test that asserts it so I can see the chain
stories → spec → tests is intact.

Do not modify tests or code.

Observe: This is the end-to-end traceability check. stories.md is the original user-facing contract; the spec refined it; the tests execute it. Seeing each criterion mapped to a specific test confirms the chain — not just "tests match the spec" but "tests match what the user actually asked for." This step only surfaces the mapping; it does not change anything.

Check the plan: did Claude tick boxes it could not actually verify?

Open docs/plans/task-comments.md and scan the checklist. Depending on the model you are running, it has been observed that Claude sometimes designates UI acceptance criteria as manual verification steps — because the project has no browser-driving harness wired up to test them automatically — and then ticks those manual items anyway as part of finishing the implementation loop. Stronger models are less prone to this; weaker ones fall into it more often. A [ ] in the plan has no format distinction between "I ran this" and "a human will run this," so once the loop enters iteration mode every unchecked box looks like progress. The app works in your browser today because Claude wrote reasonable code from a careful spec, not necessarily because anything verified the UI contract end-to-end.

This is the exact failure mode Phase 4 addresses structurally. The Ralph Loop replaces the manual checklist with a three-layer binary gate — ESLint, Jest, and Playwright driving a real browser. UI acceptance criteria become tests that either pass or fail — no self-reported [x]. When you see Ralph run in the next chapter, this is the problem it is solving: an implementation loop cannot lie about behaviour it was structurally unable to check.

Step 8: Manual verification

Open TaskFlow in your browser, click a task card to open the detail panel, and try posting a comment. Confirm it appears in the list without the page reloading, that the textarea clears after submit, and that an empty submit does nothing. This is your sanity check before the self-review — the part Claude could not verify for itself.

Key Insight

You just closed the artifact chain: human intent (Phase 1 requirements) → acceptance criteria (Phase 1 stories) → executable tests → implementation code. Every link is traceable. The tests existed before the code — they defined what 'done' means. Claude implemented to satisfy them, not the other way around.

title: Review, Commit, Advance
bodyHtml:
Review, Commit, Advance

Tests pass and the smoke test looks good. Before committing, run a self-review against the spec — not a generic code review, but a targeted check that the implementation matches the contract from Phase 2. This catches issues that tests don't cover: wrong error format, inconsistent patterns, spec deviations.

Self-review at implementation time costs roughly 5-10% of session tokens. The same review done as a separate PR review costs 50-100% (new session, re-read all code, re-learn context). Review early, review cheap.

What Claude Checks vs. What You Check

Claude Self-Review (mechanical)Your Review (semantic)
Does the implementation match every spec requirement?Is this the right approach architecturally?
Does the error format match the architecture plan?Does the business logic make sense?
Missing error handling or edge cases?Are the validation rules what stakeholders actually want?
Consistency with existing code patterns and CLAUDE.md conventions?Would you approve this in a PR?

Claude catches the 60-70% of issues that are mechanical (wrong format, missing handler, inconsistent pattern). You focus on the 30-40% that require judgment (business logic, naming, architecture). Together, the review is faster and more thorough than either alone.

The Self-Review Prompt

Here is the prompt that performs a targeted self-review:

Review the implementation you just built.

Check against:
- Feature spec: docs/specs/task-comments.md
- Architecture: docs/architecture/task-comments.md
- CLAUDE.md conventions

For each issue:
1. Severity: critical / warning / suggestion
2. File and line
3. What's wrong
4. Proposed fix

Do NOT report style issues.

You could paste this into Claude right now and get a review. But you'll run this same check after every feature — and Phase 4's Ralph Loop will run it on every deferred unit automatically. Rather than copy-paste it each time, package it as a skill once and invoke it with a slash command from then on.

Skill: Self-Review

Package the Review as a Reusable Skill

Same pattern as validate-spec and design-review: a markdown file in .claude/skills/ that becomes a slash command. Type /self-review task-comments and the review runs against that feature's artifacts.

Hands-On: Create the Skill, Then Run the Review

Step 5: Fix review findings

Ask Claude to fix all critical and warning issues:

Update the backlog to mark the ACTIVE unit as complete:

test-first pattern when its turn comes.

The Phase 3 Checkpoint

Verify what Phase 3 produced:

These artifacts feed Phase 4 (CI/CD) directly. The implementation gets validated, tested end-to-end with Playwright, containerized with Docker, and wired into a complete CI/CD pipeline.

Key Insight

Phase 3 is complete. You've gone from spec to working, tested code using one consistent methodology: acceptance criteria → tests → implementation → self-review (via skill). The artifact chain is closed — every requirement is traceable through tests to code. You now have three skills — validate-spec, design-review, self-review — all committed to your project. In Phase 4, these exact skills are reused as automated gates in the Ralph Loop pipeline.

title: Pre-Built Workflow Plugins
bodyHtml:
You Don't Have to Build Every Skill From Scratch

Across Phases 1 through 3 you packaged three quality gates as skills: validate-spec, design-review, and self-review. Every one of them started as a prompt you ran manually, then got promoted to .claude/skills/ so the team could reuse it. This is the right pattern for the prompts that are specific to your project and your quality bar.

But not every skill needs to start from your own notes. There are ready-made plugins that package entire SDLC workflows as slash commands — dozens of them, maintained by teams that have been shipping with Claude Code for months. Borrow their work rather than rediscovering it.

EPCC: Explore-Plan-Code-Commit

The EPCC (Explore-Plan-Code-Commit) plugin is one of the clearest examples. It maps almost one-to-one onto the workflow you just learned:

CommandPurposeOur Equivalent
/prdGenerate a Product Requirements DocumentPhase 1: Sources → requirements → stories
/trdGenerate a Technical Requirements DocumentPhase 2: Architecture exploration → architecture doc
/epcc-exploreMap the codebase — code archaeologistPhase 2: Codebase mapping → architecture doc
/epcc-planDesign an implementation planPhase 3: Write implementation plan
/epcc-codeImplement with auto-validationPhase 3: TDD cycle → implement → verify
/epcc-commitRun tests and commitPhase 3: Self-review → update backlog
/epcc-resumeResume interrupted work(No equivalent)

Browse the source: epcc-workflow/commands on GitHub . Each .md file is a slash command — read them to see how production teams structure their workflow prompts.

Key Takeaway

The principle matters more than the specific plugin. Your team's workflow might look different — maybe you need /threat-model or /generate-migration or /write-runbook. The building blocks are the same: a SKILL.md file in .claude/skills/ with a description and a well-crafted prompt. Start with the ones you write yourself (the three you just built), then fill in the gaps with pre-built plugins like EPCC.

Choosing Between Your Own Skills and Pre-Built Plugins

SituationRecommendation
Quality gate specific to your team's standards (review checklists, spec validation)Write your own — you know the bar
Workflow step that's generic across projects (code archaeology, commit conventions, resuming work)Use a pre-built plugin; borrow battle-tested prompts
Workflow step that's generic but you want fine control over behaviorStart from a pre-built plugin, then fork and customize
Domain-specific expertise (e.g., AWS CDK patterns, regulated-industry compliance)Look for community plugins first; if none exist, write your own

The three skills you built in this workshop fall into the first category: they encode your quality bar for specs, architecture, and implementation. They're yours to keep, version, and evolve. The EPCC-style workflow plugins fall into the second: good starting points that save you writing boilerplate prompts for generic steps.

title: SDLC 4: Ralph Wiggum Loop
bodyHtml:
Workshop 7: The Ralph Loop

From typing prompts to running a pipeline — one script builds one unit from the backlog, script-supervised, with external quality gates.

Audience: All Developers | Duration: Half day

From Typing Prompts to Running a Pipeline

In Phases 1–3 you built one feature by typing ~6 prompts interactively. It worked, but it was a one-time effort — not reusable.

The Ralph Loop turns that into a reusable pipeline. Four generic prompt files plus one bash script, pre-staged in /workshop/ralph/. Run one command: bash ../ralph/ralph.sh. The script reads the backlog, picks the next DEFERRED unit, plans it (spec + architecture, gated by your Phase 2 skills), generates failing tests, and implements one plan item per iteration with fresh context until the unit is done.

Same SDLC methodology. Same quality gates. Now it's infrastructure — add a unit to the backlog, run the script, it builds the unit. Supervised automation: you watch the terminal and can intervene, but you're not typing prompts.

What You'll Learn

  • Understand the Ralph Loop: a reusable pipeline that builds features from the backlog
  • Wire up a three-layer back-pressure stack (ESLint → Jest → Playwright) with cheap-first ordering
  • Read four generic prompt files and understand why each one exists
  • Run one script that plans, generates tests, and implements the next DEFERRED unit
  • See Phase 1–2 skills (validate-spec, design-review) reused as automated quality gates
  • Understand supervised automation: script-supervised, human watches and can intervene

Before You Start

Pick up where you left off — your taskflow folder should have the task-comments feature fully implemented from Phase 3 (requirements, spec, architecture, ADR, implementation with tests, and skills like /validate-spec, /design-review, /self-review all in place).

If the app isn't already running, start it:

npm run dev
# Open http://localhost:3000

Try the Kanban board — create a task, move it between columns. You should also see the task-comments feature working (click a task to add comments). This is the state Phase 3 left behind.

Phase Flow

Key Concepts

ConceptDescription
The Ralph LoopAutonomous bash while-loop: fresh context per iteration, one plan item at a time, external back-pressure gates.
Back-PressureQuality checks (lint, tests, E2E) running outside the agent — non-negotiable pass/fail authority.
Externalized TestsTests generated by a separate invocation before the loop starts. The implementation agent cannot modify them.
AGENT.mdSelf-improving operational knowledge. Starts with seeded conventions, grows as the loop discovers project patterns.

title: The Pattern
bodyHtml:
The Pattern

The Ralph Loop  is an autonomous coding technique by Geoffrey Huntley. The core idea: a bash loop that invokes claude -p repeatedly, with fresh context each iteration. State lives in files on disk — a plan that gets checked off, an AGENT.md that accumulates operational knowledge, and a constant PROMPT.md that drives every iteration.

In Phases 1–3 you typed prompts interactively to build one feature. The Ralph Loop turns that into a reusable pipeline: prompt files written once, then one script that builds any feature from the backlog — planning, test generation, and implementation, all automated. The script is the operator, not you. You wrote the policy; it executes.

From One Feature to a Pipeline

Phase 3 (manual)Phase 4 (Ralph pipeline)
You type ~6 prompts interactivelyYou run one script: bash ../ralph/ralph.sh
One feature, one sessionAny feature from the backlog, same script
You watch and steer between stepsScript orchestrates planning → tests → implementation
Claude tests inside its own sessionTests run outside the agent (externalized back-pressure)
Works once — not reusableSame prompts, any feature — reusable infrastructure
Key Takeaway

The value isn't 'externalized tests' or 'fresh context.' The value is: you write a set of prompt files and a script, then that script can build any feature in your backlog. Phase 3 built one unit in ~30 minutes of interactive work. The Ralph pipeline builds it from one command.

How the Pipeline Works

For the next DEFERRED unit in the backlog, the script runs three phases — the same methodology you used manually, now automated:

Supervised Automation, Not Hands-Off

Ralph is supervised automation. You run the script, watch the terminal, and can interrupt if something goes wrong. The original technique has the human monitoring output, resetting with git reset --hard when the agent goes off track, and adjusting prompts between runs. It's a power tool, not autopilot.

FileRoleChanges between iterations?
prompts/PROMPT.mdThe constant — what to do each iterationNever
docs/plans/{unit}.mdThe state machine — checked items = doneYes — items get checked off
prompts/AGENT.mdOperational knowledge the loop learnsYes — grows as the loop runs
docs/specs/{unit}.mdThe contract — what 'done' meansNo — frozen before the loop starts
.last-test-resultFailure feedback from the previous iterationYes — written on failure, deleted on pass
.ralph-active-planPlan file path (written by planning step, read by orchestrator)Once — written during planning

Back-Pressure Layers

Before running the pipeline, the project needs back-pressure — automated quality checks that run outside the agent and determine pass or fail. TaskFlow currently has Jest (from Phase 3). The Ralph pipeline adds two more layers:

1. ESLint (~1s, syntax + style) → 2. Jest (~3s, unit tests) → 3. Playwright (~15s, E2E browser tests)

The ordering is deliberate: cheapest and fastest first. If ESLint catches a syntax error, don't run Jest. If Jest fails, don't launch a browser. Each layer is a gate — fail at any layer and the loop resets.

Why Back-Pressure Runs Outside the Agent

If Claude runs its own tests, it can rationalize failures ("these tests are incorrect, let me fix them"). When the back-pressure is external, it's non-negotiable. Tests pass or they don't. The loop script decides what happens next, not the agent.

Agent runs tests (fragile)Loop runs tests (robust)
Claude decides if tests are correctShell script runs tests after Claude exits
Can modify tests to match implementationExit code is the only signal: 0 = pass
"These tests are wrong, let me update them"Tests are immutable — Claude can't touch them
No external authority on pass/failThe loop is the authority, not the agent

TRY IT: Wire up back-pressure

Everything is pre-staged in /workshop/ralph/backpressure/. You'll examine the files, run one install script to wire them into TaskFlow, then verify the three-layer stack works.

You should be in your taskflow/ folder with Phase 3 complete (task-comments shipped, tests/comments.test.js passing).

Step 1: Examine the pre-staged back-pressure files

Open these files in VS Code — read them, don't modify:

/workshop/ralph/backpressure/tests/e2e/board.spec.jsSmoke test: page loads with the three kanban columns visible
/workshop/ralph/backpressure/install.shIdempotent installer — copies configs, updates package.json, runs npm install and playwright install chromium

Nothing is generated at runtime. Nothing is typed into Claude. These are frozen, shipped, inspected.

Step 2: Run the installer

From your taskflow/ folder:

Run in terminal:

1
bash ../ralph/backpressure/install.sh

Observe: The script copies .eslintrc.json and playwright.config.js into taskflow/, copies the smoke test into tests/e2e/, adds lint and test:e2e scripts to package.json, installs eslint + @playwright/test as devDependencies, and installs the Chromium browser. Re-running it is safe — it skips files that already exist.

Step 3: Verify the three-layer stack

Before running the gate, know what's being tested:

LayerWhat runsWhere the tests live
npm run linteslint src/ on every .js under src/No test files — static analysis of your source
npm testjest --runInBand → src/__tests__/comments.test.js30 tests from Phase 3 (task-comments spec)

Jest auto-ignores tests/e2e/ (added to testPathIgnorePatterns by the installer) so Playwright specs don't get picked up twice. Once Ralph runs, it'll add a third set — src/__tests__/{unit}.test.js for whatever unit the planner picks.

Run in terminal:

1

Observe: All three layers pass in sequence. ESLint (~1s), Jest 30 tests (~3s), Playwright smoke (~15s, auto-starts the server via npm start). This is the exact sequence the Ralph pipeline runs after every implementation iteration.

Step 4: Tell CLAUDE.md about the toolchain

Every Ralph iteration starts a fresh Claude session that reads CLAUDE.md first. Make sure it advertises the toolchain. Open taskflow/CLAUDE.md and add this section (or update an existing one):

- Unit tests: `npm test` (Jest)
- E2E tests: `npm run test:e2e` (Playwright — auto-starts dev server)

Save. No Claude invocation needed — this is a 4-line edit.

Key Insight

A three-layer gate — syntax/style, functional correctness, user-visible behavior — fastest-to-slowest. It runs outside the agent, making it a non-negotiable authority on what counts as "working."

title: The Pipeline Files
bodyHtml:
Four Prompt Files and One Script

The pipeline is five files in /workshop/ralph/ — four prompts and one shell script. Each prompt handles a different phase of the SDLC; the script orchestrates them. Everything is pre-staged. You won't type prompts into Claude in this page — you'll open each file, read it, understand why it exists, and move on.

FileRole
plan.mdPlanning prompt: reads the backlog, picks the next DEFERRED unit, produces spec + architecture + implementation plan
generate-tests.mdTest generation prompt: reads the spec, produces failing tests
PROMPT.mdImplementation constant: picks one plan item, implements it, checks it off
AGENT.mdOperational knowledge — seeded with project conventions, grown by the loop
ralph.shOrchestrator: wraps the three prompt phases in a while-loop with back-pressure gates

TRY IT: Open and read each file

These files are in /workshop/ralph/. Open them in VS Code one at a time as you read this page. Do not modify them.

1. ralph/plan.md

The planning prompt. Key properties:

  • Reads the backlog, doesn't synthesize requirements. The backlog is authoritative — the stories and ACs are already there from Phase 1. Re-deriving them from raw sources is wasted work and risks drift.
  • Uses task-comments artifacts as format exemplars. The spec, architecture, and plan you wrote in Phase 2–3 are the templates — same structure, same depth. No prose instructions on "what makes a good spec" — just "match this file." Output goes to docs/specs/{unit}.md, docs/architecture/{unit}.md, and docs/plans/{unit}.md.
  • Runs your Phase 2 quality gates. /validate-spec and /design-review are the same skills you invoked manually. The loop is their second consumer.
  • Plans are implementation-only. No "run tests", "verify tests pass", or "update backlog" steps — the orchestrator handles gates and backlog updates automatically. No conditional items either — split into concrete steps or omit.
  • Writes .ralph-active-plan as its final step — the plan file path (e.g. docs/plans/error-hardening.md). The orchestrator reads this to drive the implementation loop.

2. ralph/generate-tests.md

The test generation prompt. Very short by design:

  • Reads CLAUDE.md to find the active unit.
  • Idempotent: First checks if test files for the unit already exist (src/__tests__/{unit}.test.js, tests/e2e/{unit}.spec.js). If they exist and cover all ACs, it skips generation and checks off any corresponding plan items that are already done.
  • Otherwise generates Jest tests for API/backend ACs under src/__tests__/, Playwright tests for UI ACs under tests/e2e/.
  • New tests must fail. Existing tests must still pass. That's the entire contract.

Why so short? The spec already defines what the tests have to verify. The prompt just names the output locations and the pass/fail shape.

3. ralph/PROMPT.md

The implementation constant — every loop iteration reads this exact file. Key properties:

  • Finds the first - [ ] in the plan, implements only that item. One step at a time, fresh context each time. No drift from "I'm on step 1" into "while I'm here, let me also do step 3."
  • Tests are frozen. The prompt forbids modifying anything under tests/. Tests are the contract — if Claude could edit them, they stop being a contract.
  • Do NOT commit. The orchestrator commits after gates pass — Claude's job is implementation only.
  • Self-updates AGENT.md. When the model discovers something useful (build quirk, file convention, library gotcha), it appends to AGENT.md under "Learned." That knowledge persists across iterations and across units.
  • .last-test-result as a signal. If the current plan item is a verification step ("verify tests pass", "run tests"), Claude checks whether .last-test-result exists. The orchestrator deletes this file when gates pass and writes it when they fail — so its presence = "still broken" and its absence = "all passed." This prevents Claude from blindly checking off verification items when gates actually failed.

4. ralph/AGENT.md

Operational knowledge — seeded with TaskFlow's build commands and conventions, grown by the loop. Two sections:

  • Build & Test / Conventions — seeded. "UI is a single-page app in public/index.html", "storage reads/writes go through src/data/store.js", etc.
  • Learned — empty at start. Entries appear as the loop discovers patterns.

This is the memory that isn't in CLAUDE.md and isn't in the spec. It's the folk knowledge — the stuff you only learn by actually building something.

5. ralph/ralph.sh

The orchestrator. Open it and trace the control flow:

  • Outer loop: up to MAX_UNITS passes. On each pass, check the backlog for a DEFERRED unit. If none, exit. Otherwise: plan → generate tests → run implementation loop.
  • Reads .ralph-active-plan after the planning step to locate the plan file. If the file is missing, the script errors out — planning must write it.
  • Inner loop: up to MAX_IMPL_ITERATIONS passes. Each iteration runs claude -p PROMPT.md, then the three gates (ESLint → Jest → Playwright). On failure, write .last-test-result and continue. On success, delete .last-test-result, commit, and check if any - [ ] items remain in the plan — if none, break out; otherwise continue.
  • Auto-commits: The script commits after test generation and after each iteration where gates pass. Claude never commits — separation of concerns.
  • Backlog update: When all plan items are checked off, the script marks the unit COMPLETE in requirements/backlog.md directly (via sed). This used to be a plan item delegated to Claude — now the orchestrator owns it.
  • --step mode: pauses after each phase for review. Essential for the first run.
  • Symlink trick: on startup, ralph.sh creates taskflow/prompts as a symlink to /workshop/ralph/. That way the prompts can reference paths like prompts/AGENT.md from inside the taskflow working directory.

MAX_UNITS defaults to 1. You can bump it via env var (MAX_UNITS=3 bash ../ralph/ralph.sh) to build multiple units in one run — useful once you trust the pipeline.

Key Insight

Four generic files and one script. None of them mention task-comments or any other unit name. They read the backlog and CLAUDE.md to figure out what's active. Write once, run on any feature.

Why Pre-Staged?

Phase 3 had you cat > SKILL.md <<EOF via the shell. Why not do the same here?

Because the lesson in Phase 4 isn't "how to write the PROMPT.md character by character." The lesson is: the pipeline is small — five files — and the architecture of those five files matters more than the exact wording. Opening finished files lets you see the whole shape at once. You'd get the wording right on your second or third rewrite anyway; the structure is what you need to learn.

Everything you read in this page is plain markdown and bash. Fork it, tune it, port it to a different project — the ideas are small enough to internalize in one reading.

title: Run the Pipeline
bodyHtml:
Run the Pipeline on the Next DEFERRED Unit

Your back-pressure stack is wired. Your prompts and script are sitting in /workshop/ralph/. Time to run it. For this workshop we build one unit — whichever unit is next DEFERRED in requirements/backlog.md. After Phase 3 that will be error-hardening (unless you changed the backlog).

You'll run in --step mode first — pauses between phases so you can review output before continuing. That's where prompt issues are cheapest to catch.

TRY IT: Run Ralph

Step 1: Run in step mode

Run in terminal:

1
bash ../ralph/ralph.sh --step

Observe: The pipeline pauses after each phase.

After planning: Check docs/specs/{unit}.md and docs/plans/{unit}.md — is the spec tight? Are the acceptance criteria numbered and testable? Is the plan atomic (each item independently implementable)? If something looks wrong, Ctrl+C, fix the prompt, re-run.

After test generation: Run npm test — the new tests/{unit}.test.js tests should fail, the existing 30 tests/comments.test.js tests should still pass. If new tests don't fail, the generator didn't produce tests that exercise the spec.

After each implementation iteration: Check the plan file — did exactly one - [ ] become - [x]? Check prompts/AGENT.md — did the model learn anything new? If a gate failed, .last-test-result has the output.

Press Enter to continue at each pause. When the plan has no more unchecked items, the unit is done and the script exits.

Step 2: Review what the pipeline produced

Start Claude Code and ask it to summarize:

Run in terminal:

1
claude

Tell Claude:

Summarize what changed in the project:
1. Which unit is now COMPLETE in requirements/backlog.md?
2. Show the final docs/plans/{unit}.md — how many iterations did it take?
3. What did prompts/AGENT.md learn? (diff the "Learned" section against the initial file)
4. Run npm run lint && npm test && npm run test:e2e — do all gates pass?

Observe: The backlog shows the unit flipped from DEFERRED to COMPLETE. The plan has all items checked off. AGENT.md has new entries. All three gates pass.

What Just Happened

You wrote four prompt files and a shell script (or in this workshop, read them). That's the infrastructure. One command ran the full SDLC for one unit — planning, architecture, spec validation, design review, test generation, implementation, and backlog update — all on fresh Claude contexts, gated by external tests.

ArtifactLocationCreated by
Specdocs/specs/{unit}.mdplan.md → validated by /validate-spec
Architecturedocs/architecture/{unit}.mdplan.md → reviewed by /design-review
Implementation plandocs/plans/{unit}.mdplan.md, checked off by the implementation loop
Testssrc/__tests__/{unit}.test.js and possibly tests/e2e/{unit}.spec.jsgenerate-tests.md (immutable once written)
Source codesrc/ and/or public/PROMPT.md loop, gated by ESLint + Jest + Playwright
Backlog updaterequirements/backlog.mdralph.sh marks the unit COMPLETE after all plan items are done

Same methodology as Phases 1-3. Same quality gates. Now run from one command.

Going Further

Build more units in one run. The script takes a MAX_UNITS env var. Bump it to run multiple units back-to-back — AGENT.md accumulates knowledge across units, so unit 2 is faster than unit 1:

1
MAX_UNITS=3 bash ../ralph/ralph.sh

Run fully automated. Drop --step to run end-to-end without pauses. Watch the terminal, ready to Ctrl+C if the pipeline goes off track.

Adapt to your own project. The files in /workshop/ralph/ are intentionally small. The planning prompt reads whatever backlog you give it, the test prompt targets whatever test framework is in CLAUDE.md, the implementation prompt works with any plan file. Fork, tune, port.

Ralph's Limits

Ralph converges on "tests pass." It has no signal for anything tests don't measure: visual consistency, code style coherence, documentation quality, whether the UI matches the rest of the app. For a backend feature with comprehensive tests, that's fine. For UI work, you'll still want a human in the loop — or an evaluator that grades the subjective qualities, which is a different tool for a different job.

Key Insight

The pipeline built a full SDLC cycle from one command. The cost was five files. That's the trade Ralph offers — authoring a policy once, then letting the script execute it over any feature you add to the backlog.

Congratulations — you have completed the AI-Powered SDLC workshop.

Across this workshop, you produced a complete artifact chain — every phase feeding the next:

The workshop followed a deliberate arc:

  1. Understand the tool (Fundamentals) — How Claude Code thinks, how to configure it, how to extend it

  3. Automate it (Phase 4) — Write prompt files once, run a script that builds features from the backlog

Each level builds on the previous. The skills from Phases 1-3 became automated quality gates in Phase 4's pipeline. The CLAUDE.md you wrote in Phase 2 became the configuration that every Ralph Loop iteration reads.
